findings.title: Preference Against Coercion
findings.claim: The focus says Allah preferred Joseph over the brothers. In 20:72, speakers refuse to prefer a coercive ruler over clear signs and their Creator; the shared preference relation makes the focus legible in a wider pattern where what receives precedence matters.
findings.mechanism: The focus verb آثَرَكَ, with Joseph as its object and عَلَيْنَا as the comparison, states Allah's preference of Joseph over the brothers. The exact 20:72 surface has a group refusing to prefer its ruler over clear signs and the One who created it. This independent cross-surah trigger returns through the focus preference verb and shifts attention from rank alone to the grounds of preference.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see preference as a comparative ordering whose object and grounds matter, rather than treating every unequal ranking as the same kind of claim.
findings.containment: The focus's ordinary comparison remains intact. The magicians' refusal and God's preference are not assigned the same motive, and no wider narrative identity or cross-surah channel is claimed.

epistemic.reason: The focus occurrence, comparison, and accepted branch are supplied, and the trusted cross-run record nominates the focus reading. The external ayah is supplied as exact Arabic without target morphology or lexical analysis, so the comparison remains qualified.

findings.title: Confession Across Error and Culpability
findings.claim: The brothers' plural self-description keeps both an unintended failure to reach the right and culpable wrongdoing in view. Wider confessional passages pair error with forgetting or ignorance and pair acknowledged wrongs with a separate reference to coercion, allowing moral responsibility to remain visible without deciding the brothers' intent.
findings.mechanism: The focus active participle خَٰطِـِٔينَ names the speakers as wrongdoers. The supplied focus branches preserve an unintended-miss reading and a culpable-sin reading. The 2:286 and 6:54 contexts keep error under forgetting or ignorance available; 20:73 and 96:16 provide separate contexts of admitted wrong and sinful conduct. These contacts return through the focus predicate and make uncertainty about intent part of the reading rather than a reason to choose one branch.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hold the force of the brothers' self-accusation together with uncertainty about how knowingly each wrong was done.
findings.containment: The focus does not say that the brothers were coerced, innocent, or ignorant when they acted. The other passages are analogies, not facts about Yusuf's brothers, and neither branch is ranked.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology, word alignment, and both branch records are supplied; the trusted cross-run nomination maps the confession to those carriers. findings.title: A Wider Horizon of Brotherly Repair

findings.reader_payoff: The admission can be heard as part of a broader movement toward restored relation, rather than only as a final label of guilt.
findings.containment: The 59:10 speakers are a different community and their prayer is not a report of what Joseph's brothers or Joseph did. The focus states confession, not forgiveness or completed reconciliation.

findings.containment: The 26:97 group is not identified with the brothers. The focus's pronoun shifts do not prove a deliberate social reclassification or a completed change in relationships.
